questions.stem: An 83 year old woman has a 1 day history of a painful, swollen left knee. She is sweaty and cannot stand. Her temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. The knee is hot, red and tender, held flexed, and any movement causes severe pain. There is no history of trauma.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A single hot, swollen, immobile knee with high fever and hypotension is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Crystal arthritis mimics it but rarely makes the patient septic.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Hot, swollen, immobile joint plus systemic sepsis signs.

elim: Cellulitis does not stop all joint movement or cause a tense effusion.
Gout can mimic it, but fever with hypotension and sweating points to sepsis; it must be excluded by aspiration.
Osteoarthritis is not hot, red or febrile.
Pseudogout rarely causes hypotension and systemic sepsis.

steps.x: **E. Septic arthritis.** The knee is the commonest joint. Hot joint plus systemic signs: aspirate.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with rheumatoid arthritis has a 2 day history of a hot, swollen right knee. He takes methotrexate and prednisolone 7.5 mg daily. His temperature is 38.7°C and pulse rate 106 bpm. Synovial fluid is turbid and yellow. Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. He has never had MRSA.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Gram-positive cocci in clusters are staphylococci. S. aureus, mostly MSSA, is the commonest cause overall and in older patients.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Clusters mean staphylococci; no MRSA history.

elim: E. coli is a Gram-negative rod.
Gonococcus is a Gram-negative diplococcus in young, sexually active patients.
Pseudomonas is a Gram-negative rod, classically in IV drug users.
Streptococci form chains, not clusters.

steps.x: **B. Methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus.** S. aureus (MSSA) is the commonest cause, especially in the elderly.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has a 3 day history of a hot, swollen left wrist. She has had rheumatoid arthritis for 20 years, which has recently been treated with methotrexate and a reducing course of prednisolone. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine and a BMI of 29. Her temperature is 38.4°C. Septic arthritis is confirmed on aspiration.
questions.q: Which is the most important risk factor for this infection?
questions.e: Pre-existing joint disease such as RA, especially when immunosuppressed with methotrexate or steroids, is a major risk factor for septic arthritis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Damaged joint plus immunosuppression.

elim: Age alone is a weak factor compared with immunosuppressed joint disease.
Calcium channel blockers do not predispose to joint infection.
Sex is not a recognised risk factor.
Obesity is a weak factor at most.

steps.x: **D. Immunosuppressed rheumatoid arthritis.** Risk factors: IV drug use, joint disease (RA on methotrexate/steroids), prosthetic joints, immunosuppression.

questions.stem: A 4 year old boy has a 2 day history of right hip pain and now refuses to bear weight on his right leg. His temperature is 39.1°C and pulse rate 136 bpm. The right hip is held flexed and externally rotated, and movement is very painful.

visual.title: Kocher's criteria score
visual.label: 4 points
visual.caption: All four criteria met: 99% probability of septic arthritis.

questions.q: Using Kocher's criteria, which is the probability that he has septic arthritis?
questions.e: He is non-weight bearing, febrile above 38.5°C, WCC above 12 and ESR above 40: 4 of 4 Kocher points, a 99% probability of septic arthritis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Count each of the 4 criteria: non-weight bearing, fever >38.5°C, WCC >12, ESR >40.

elim: That is 1 point; he scores all 4.
That is 2 points.
That is 3 points.
That is 0 points.

questions.stem: A 7 year old girl has a 1 day history of a painful left hip and is limping but can still walk with help. Her temperature is 38.8°C and pulse rate 118 bpm. Hip movement is reduced. Investigations: white cell count 13.6 ×10⁹/L (5.0–14.5), ESR 22 mm/hr (<10), CRP 31 mg/L (<5).
questions.q: Using Kocher's criteria, which is the probability that she has septic arthritis?
questions.e: She has fever above 38.5°C and WCC above 12 (2 points) but is weight bearing with an ESR below 40: 2 points is a 40% probability.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Fever and WCC score; walking and ESR 22 do not.

elim: That is 1 point; she scores 2.
That needs 3 points; she is weight bearing and ESR is below 40.
That needs all 4 points.
That is 0 points.

steps.x: **B. 40%.** Two Kocher points = 40% probability: still aspirate.

questions.stem: A 3 year old boy has a 2 day history of a new limp and now will not stand on his left leg. His temperature is 38.9°C. Investigations: white cell count 15.2 ×10⁹/L (5.0–15.0), ESR 28 mm/hr (<10), CRP 64 mg/L (<5). An ultrasound shows a left hip effusion.
questions.q: Using Kocher's criteria, which is the probability that he has septic arthritis?
questions.e: Non-weight bearing, fever above 38.5°C and WCC above 12 give 3 points (ESR 28 does not score): a 93% probability.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: will not stand on his left leg
steps.x: Three of four criteria; ESR does not reach 40.

elim: That is 1 point.
That is 2 points.
ESR is below 40, so he does not score 4.
That is 0 points.

steps.x: **C. 93%.** Three Kocher points = 93%. CRP is not one of Kocher's criteria.

questions.stem: A 5 year old girl has a 3 day history of a limp after a cold. She is walking, though with a limp. Her temperature is 37.4°C. The right hip has slightly reduced internal rotation. Investigations: white cell count 8.9 ×10⁹/L (5.0–14.5), ESR 12 mm/hr (<10), CRP 9 mg/L (<5).
questions.q: Using Kocher's criteria, which is the best interpretation of her risk of septic arthritis?
questions.e: She is weight bearing, afebrile, WCC normal and ESR below 40: 0 Kocher points, very low risk, so transient synovitis is the likely cause.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
None of the four criteria are met.

elim: That is 1 point; she scores none.
That is 2 points.
That is 3 points.
That is 4 points.

steps.x: **E. Very low; transient synovitis likely.** Kocher's criteria stratify septic arthritis against transient synovitis in children.

questions.stem: A 21 year old woman has a 5 day history of pain moving between her wrists, ankles and fingers. She now has a hot, swollen right knee. There is tenosynovitis over the back of the left hand and a few painless pustules on her forearms. She has a new sexual partner. Her temperature is 38.3°C and pulse rate 98 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis and skin pustules before settling in one joint is disseminated gonococcal infection, the commonest cause in young, sexually active patients.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: pain moving between her wrists, ankles and fingers
steps.x: Migratory joint pain, tenosynovitis, dermatitis, young and sexually active.

elim: Chlamydia causes reactive arthritis, not pustules, tenosynovitis and a septic joint.
Pseudomonas is linked with IV drug use.
S. aureus causes a single septic joint without migratory pain or pustules.
Streptococcal arthritis follows soft tissue infection or pharyngitis.

steps.x: **B. Neisseria gonorrhoeae.** Gonococcal arthritis: arthralgia, tenosynovitis, dermatitis, then one joint.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man has a 2 day history of a hot, swollen left ankle. Last week he had a painful, swollen right testis and a burning sensation passing urine. His temperature is 38.1°C and pulse rate 96 bpm. The ankle is aspirated and the fluid sent for urgent microscopy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on Gram stain of the synovial fluid?
questions.e: Epididymo-orchitis and urethritis before a septic joint in a young man point to Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a Gram-negative diplococcus.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Urethritis and epididymo-orchitis in a young man.

elim: Rods suggest Pseudomonas or coliforms.
Chains are streptococci.
Clusters are staphylococci.
Those are urate crystals in gout, not a Gram stain finding.

steps.x: **A. Gram-negative diplococci.** Gonococcus = Gram-negative diplococci (though the Gram stain can be negative).

questions.stem: A 31 year old man who injects heroin has a 3 day history of a painful, swollen left knee. He is sweating profusely and disorientated to time. His temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. There are track marks on both arms. Synovial fluid Gram stain shows Gram-negative rods.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Gram-negative rods in an IV drug user with confusion and sweating point to Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
IV drug use, confusion and sweating, Gram-negative rods.

elim: E. coli is not the classic organism in IV drug users.
H. influenzae is rare and seen in unvaccinated young children.
Gonococci are diplococci, not rods.
S. aureus is a Gram-positive coccus, though it is also common in IV drug users.

steps.x: **D. Pseudomonas aeruginosa.** Pseudomonas in IV drug users; S. aureus is the overall commonest.

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman had cellulitis of her right shin 2 weeks ago that was treated with oral antibiotics. She now has a 2 day history of a hot, swollen right knee and cannot bear weight. Her temperature is 38.6°C. Synovial fluid is turbid and Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in chains.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Gram-positive cocci in chains after a soft tissue infection point to a Streptococcus species.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Preceding soft tissue infection, chains on Gram stain.

elim: Gonococci are Gram-negative diplococci.
Pseudomonas is a Gram-negative rod.
S. aureus forms clusters, not chains.
Coagulase-negative staphylococci form clusters and infect prosthetic joints.

steps.x: **E. Streptococcus species.** Streptococci follow soft tissue infection, pharyngitis or trauma.

questions.stem: A 2 year old girl has a 1 day history of a new limp and now cries when her left leg is moved. She has been irritable and off her food. Her temperature is 39.0°C and pulse rate 150 bpm. She holds the left hip flexed and abducted and resists any passive movement. She has no history of injury.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A febrile toddler with a new limp who resists all hip movement has septic arthritis until proven otherwise.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Children present with a new-onset limp; high fever and refusal to move.

elim: JIA is chronic, not an acute febrile illness.
Perthes affects 4 to 8 year olds with an insidious, afebrile limp.
There was no injury, and a fracture does not cause a fever of 39°C.
Transient synovitis is usually afebrile or low-grade with the child still walking.

steps.x: **C. Septic arthritis.** In children, septic arthritis presents as a new limp; use Kocher's criteria against transient synovitis.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has a 2 day history of a hot, swollen right knee. He is unable to bear weight. His temperature is 38.9°C and pulse rate 110 bpm. He has no history of gout. The knee is aspirated in theatre before antibiotics and the fluid is sent to the laboratory.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on synovial fluid analysis?
o: Clear, straw-coloured fluid with 300 white cells/mm³
Purulent fluid with 80,000 white cells/mm³, over 90% neutrophils
Yellow fluid with 4,000 white cells/mm³, mostly lymphocytes
questions.e: Septic synovial fluid is purulent and yellow with a very high white cell count, usually above 10,000/mm³, over 90% neutrophils.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
A septic picture: expect pus.

elim: That is normal or non-inflammatory fluid.
That is haemarthrosis after trauma or with anticoagulation.
Those are calcium pyrophosphate crystals in pseudogout.
That is mildly inflammatory fluid, not septic.

steps.x: **D. Purulent fluid with 80,000 white cells/mm³, over 90% neutrophils.** Septic fluid: purulent, WCC above 10,000 (up to 100,000), neutrophils >90%, positive Gram stain/culture.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man with type 2 diabetes has a 2 day history of a painful right knee. He had a steroid injection into the knee for osteoarthritis 6 days ago. His temperature is 38.4°C and pulse rate 104 bpm. He cannot bear weight on the right leg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the right knee?
o: Crepitus with full range of movement
Hot, swollen knee with severely reduced range of movement
Localised swelling over the patella with full flexion
Medial joint line tenderness with locking
questions.e: A septic joint is hot, swollen, tender and immobile, with a severely reduced range of movement.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Recent joint injection, fever, cannot weight-bear.

elim: That is osteoarthritis without infection.
That is prepatellar bursitis, which spares the joint.
That is a meniscal tear.
That suggests DVT, not a joint infection.

steps.x: **B. Hot, swollen knee with severely reduced range of movement.** Septic joint: hot, swollen, immobile, tender, reduced range of movement.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman had a left total hip replacement 18 months ago. She has a 4 day history of increasing left hip pain and cannot bear weight. She has no history of a fall. Her temperature is 38.5°C and pulse rate 108 bpm. The wound is healed but the hip is very painful to move. Her CRP is 186 mg/L (<5).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Septic arthritis of the prosthetic joint
questions.e: Prosthetic joints are a major risk factor; fever, a very raised CRP and a painful, immobile hip point to septic arthritis of the prosthesis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Prosthesis, fever, raised CRP.

elim: Loosening is painful but does not cause fever and a CRP of 186.
There was no fall and the leg position is not described as abnormal.
There was no trauma.
Bursitis does not cause fever and inability to weight-bear.

steps.x: **D. Septic arthritis of the prosthetic joint.** Prosthetic joints are vulnerable because bacteria form biofilms on the implant.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has a 1 day history of a hot, swollen left knee. He cannot bear weight. His temperature is 38.7°C and pulse rate 106 bpm. Blood tests show a white cell count of 15.9 ×10⁹/L and CRP 140 mg/L. Blood cultures have been taken.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Joint aspiration with synovial fluid culture
Plain X-ray of the left knee
questions.e: Joint aspiration with culture is the gold standard: it confirms infection and identifies the organism and its sensitivities.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.
Suspected septic joint; bloods already done.

elim: MRI shows an effusion but cannot identify the organism.
X-ray is often normal early and does not diagnose infection.
Urate is unreliable and does not exclude infection.
Ultrasound can guide aspiration but does not diagnose infection.

steps.x: **A. Joint aspiration with synovial fluid culture.** Gold standard: joint aspiration with culture.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man had a right total knee replacement 2 years ago. He has a 3 day history of a hot, swollen right knee and a temperature of 38.3°C. He is haemodynamically stable. The orthopaedic team plans to aspirate the joint before giving antibiotics.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate setting for the aspiration?
o: At the bedside in the emergency department
By the patient's district nurse at home
In an operating theatre under sterile conditions
In the radiology department after 48 hours of antibiotics
questions.e: Aspiration of a prosthetic joint should be done before antibiotics, in a sterile environment such as theatre, to avoid introducing organisms.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.

clues: aspirate the joint before giving antibiotics
steps.x: A prosthetic joint must not be contaminated.

elim: A non-sterile setting risks introducing organisms into the prosthesis.
This needs urgent hospital assessment.
Not appropriate or sterile.
Antibiotics first reduce culture yield.

steps.x: **D. In an operating theatre under sterile conditions.** Aspirate before antibiotics in a sterile environment (e.g. theatre).

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has a 1 day history of a hot, swollen right knee. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. She looks well otherwise. The foundation doctor has prescribed IV flucloxacillin and is about to give the first dose. The joint has not been aspirated.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
o: Give the antibiotic and aspirate the joint in 48 hours
Give the antibiotic and request an MRI
Give the antibiotic only if blood cultures are positive
Hold the antibiotic until the joint is aspirated
Start oral colchicine and review in 24 hours
questions.e: In a stable patient, the joint is aspirated urgently before antibiotics so the organism can be grown and its sensitivities found.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.

clues: about to give the first dose
steps.x: Stable patient, no aspirate yet.

elim: Antibiotics first will sterilise the culture.
MRI does not identify the organism.
Blood cultures are often negative; this delays treatment.
This treats gout and leaves sepsis untreated.

steps.x: **D. Hold the antibiotic until the joint is aspirated.** Aspirate first, then start antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man is on day 5 of IV flucloxacillin for Staphylococcus aureus septic arthritis of the left knee. The team wants to know whether he is responding to treatment. His temperature today is 37.6°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which blood tests are most useful for monitoring his response to treatment?
questions.e: CRP and white cell count are the blood tests that track infection; failure to settle prompts orthopaedic review for washout.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.

clues: whether he is responding to treatment
steps.x: Monitoring inflammatory markers.

elim: ANA is for connective tissue disease.
RF is for rheumatoid arthritis and does not change with infection.
Urate is for gout.
These are not infection markers.

steps.x: **B. CRP and white cell count.** Bloods in septic arthritis: CRP and WBC; if not settling, consider washout.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has a 2 day history of a hot, swollen left knee. His temperature is 38.6°C. The knee is aspirated: the fluid is turbid and yellow with a white cell count of 62,000/mm³, 94% neutrophils, and no crystals. The Gram stain shows no organisms. Culture is pending. He has no allergies or MRSA history.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: The Gram stain is negative in around 30 to 50% of septic arthritis. Purulent, neutrophil-rich fluid still needs empirical IV flucloxacillin while culture is awaited.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Septic fluid, negative Gram stain, no allergy.

elim: Purulent fluid means a septic joint until culture says otherwise.
Steroid into an infected joint is dangerous.
There are no crystals; this is not gout.
A negative Gram stain occurs in 30 to 50%; delay destroys cartilage.

steps.x: **C. Start IV flucloxacillin.** Negative Gram stain does not exclude septic arthritis; start IV flucloxacillin.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy has a 1 day history of right hip pain and refuses to walk. His temperature is 38.9°C. The paediatric registrar wants to calculate his Kocher score and has requested a full blood count.
questions.q: Which other blood test is needed to complete the score?
questions.e: Kocher's criteria are non-weight bearing, fever above 38.5°C, WCC above 12 ×10⁹/L and ESR above 40 mm/hr: the ESR completes the score.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.
WCC comes from the FBC; the other blood marker is missing.

elim: Not part of Kocher's criteria.
Useful, but not part of the score.
CRP is used in some modified scores but is not one of Kocher's four criteria.
Not part of Kocher's criteria.

steps.x: **D. ESR.** Kocher: non-weight bearing, fever >38.5°C, WCC >12, ESR >40.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman from a care home has septic arthritis of the right knee. The joint has been aspirated and fluid sent for Gram stain and culture. A nasal swab last month grew MRSA. She has no drug allergies. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic?
questions.e: First-line is IV flucloxacillin, but with MRSA risk (or penicillin allergy) IV vancomycin is used instead.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
MRSA carriage, no allergy.

elim: Ceftriaxone does not cover MRSA.
Flucloxacillin does not cover MRSA.
Oral therapy is not adequate initial treatment for a septic joint.
Oral therapy alone is not adequate initial treatment for a septic joint.

steps.x: **C. IV vancomycin.** MRSA risk or penicillin allergy: IV vancomycin.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has a 2 day history of a hot, swollen left ankle. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg. The ankle has just been aspirated and Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. He has no drug allergies and has never had MRSA.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial antibiotic?
questions.e: After aspiration, empirical IV flucloxacillin is first-line for septic arthritis, covering S. aureus.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Aspirated already; staphylococci; no allergy or MRSA.

elim: Reserved for penicillin allergy or MRSA risk.
Oral antibiotics are too weak initially, and amoxicillin is not anti-staphylococcal.
Oral and not first-line.
The oral switch comes after at least 2 weeks of IV treatment.

steps.x: **A. IV flucloxacillin.** First-line: IV flucloxacillin after aspiration.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman is admitted with septic arthritis of the right knee caused by methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. She is started on IV flucloxacillin and her fever settles over 3 days. She asks how long her antibiotic course will be in total. Her CRP is falling.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic course?
o: IV for 2 weeks, then oral for a further 4–6 weeks
IV for 3 days, then oral for 7 days
questions.e: Septic arthritis is treated with IV antibiotics for at least 2 weeks followed by oral antibiotics for a further 4 to 6 weeks.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.

clues: how long her antibiotic course will be in total
steps.x: Total duration, uncomplicated course.

elim: Far too short for a joint infection.
Far too short.
Unnecessarily long IV therapy.
Oral alone is inadequate initially.

steps.x: **A. IV for 2 weeks, then oral for a further 4–6 weeks.** At least 2 weeks IV, then 4–6 weeks oral.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man is on day 6 of IV flucloxacillin for septic arthritis of the left knee. Culture grew a fully sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. He still has fevers each evening and the knee remains hot and swollen. His temperature is 38.4°C and pulse rate 104 bpm. His CRP trend is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: CRP on IV flucloxacillin
visual.caption: CRP is not settling despite 6 days of the right antibiotic.

questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Continuing fevers and inflammatory markers not settling despite appropriate antibiotics need orthopaedic review for joint washout.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Right antibiotic, sensitive organism, still not settling.

elim: Adding a drug does not drain the infected joint.
Steroid into an infected joint worsens it.
Stopping antibiotics is dangerous.
He is not improving; switching to oral is premature.

steps.x: **C. Orthopaedic review for joint washout.** Failing to improve on antibiotics: orthopaedic review for washout.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman is admitted with septic arthritis of the right knee. The joint has been aspirated and IV flucloxacillin started. She is in severe pain at rest and on any movement. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
questions.q: In addition to antibiotics, which is the most appropriate initial supportive management?
o: Analgesia and initial immobilisation of the knee
Physiotherapy with full weight bearing today
Tight compression bandage and ice only
questions.e: Supportive care in septic arthritis is analgesia and initial immobilisation, alongside IV antibiotics and joint drainage.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.

clues: severe pain at rest and on any movement
steps.x: Antibiotics started; she needs comfort and joint protection.

elim: Steroid into an infected joint is contraindicated.
Colchicine treats gout, not infection.
Early full loading of an acutely infected joint worsens pain.
Not adequate analgesia.

steps.x: **A. Analgesia and initial immobilisation of the knee.** Supportive care: analgesia and initial immobilisation.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man sees his GP with a 1 day history of a hot, swollen right knee. He cannot bear weight. His temperature is 38.6°C and pulse rate 104 bpm. He has had no injury and no previous joint problems. The GP suspects septic arthritis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Prescribe oral flucloxacillin and review in 48 hours
Prescribe oral naproxen and review in 1 week
Same-day referral for urgent orthopaedic review
questions.e: Septic arthritis is a medical emergency; delay risks irreversible joint damage, so he needs urgent same-day orthopaedic review for aspiration.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Suspected septic joint in primary care.

elim: Blind oral antibiotics delay diagnosis and treatment.
Delay risks irreversible joint damage.
This is far too slow.
X-ray will not help and delays treatment.

steps.x: **E. Same-day referral for urgent orthopaedic review.** Medical emergency: urgent orthopaedic review, aspiration, then IV antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has septic arthritis of the left knee. He has been on IV flucloxacillin for 5 days and the knee has been aspirated three times, each time producing pus, but the large effusion keeps reaccumulating. His temperature is 37.9°C and pulse rate 96 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Wait for culture sensitivities before any change
questions.e: If the effusion persists despite serial aspirations, surgical joint washout and drainage is indicated.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Repeated aspirations have not controlled the pus.

elim: Not standard management.
The joint is still infected.
Arthroplasty into an infected joint is contraindicated.
Waiting while pus reaccumulates lets it destroy cartilage.

steps.x: **C. Surgical washout of the joint.** Persistent effusion despite serial aspirations: surgical washout.

questions.stem: An 8 year old boy has a 10 day history of pain above his right knee, now with a hot, swollen knee joint. His temperature is 38.7°C. An MRI shows osteomyelitis of the distal femoral metaphysis extending into the knee joint. He has had no injury, injection or surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route by which bacteria reached the joint space?
questions.e: Bacteria reach a joint by haematogenous spread, direct inoculation, or contiguous spread from adjacent osteomyelitis, as here.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.

clues: osteomyelitis of the distal femoral metaphysis extending into the knee joint
steps.x: The infection began in the bone next to the joint.

elim: He has had no injection.
There was no injury.
Lymphatic spread is not a recognised route.
That is reactive arthritis, which is sterile.

steps.x: **A. Contiguous spread from adjacent osteomyelitis.** Routes: haematogenous, direct inoculation, contiguous from osteomyelitis.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman with no other medical problems had an intra-articular steroid injection into her left knee for osteoarthritis 4 days ago. She now has a hot, swollen knee and a temperature of 38.5°C. Culture of the synovial fluid grows Staphylococcus aureus, the same organism found on her skin swab.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route of infection?
o: Sterile reaction to the steroid crystals
questions.e: An injection can directly inoculate skin organisms such as S. aureus into the joint.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.

clues: same organism found on her skin swab
steps.x: A recent needle into the joint with a skin organism.

elim: There is no bone infection.
There is no source in the blood described.
That explains guttate psoriasis, not joint sepsis.
Culture is positive, so it is infection.

steps.x: **B. Direct inoculation during the injection.** Direct inoculation: trauma, surgery or injection.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man has septic arthritis of the right knee diagnosed 6 days after symptoms began. Synovial fluid has a white cell count of 95,000/mm³. His temperature is 38.9°C. The registrar explains that every hour of delay matters because the infection can destroy the joint surface.
questions.q: Which cell type dominates the inflammatory response that damages the joint?
questions.e: Bacterial proliferation triggers an intense neutrophilic response; bacterial toxins and host proteolytic enzymes then rapidly degrade articular cartilage, so it is an emergency.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.
Very high synovial WCC in acute bacterial infection.

elim: Eosinophils feature in allergy and parasites.
Mast cells drive allergic reactions.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with a right total knee replacement has had 3 weeks of IV antibiotics for Staphylococcus aureus infection of the joint. The organism is fully sensitive and blood levels of the antibiotic are adequate, but the infection keeps returning. She asks why the antibiotics have not cleared it.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Bacteria form a biofilm on the implant surface
Poor oral absorption of the antibiotic
The infection is caused by a virus
questions.e: Bacteria form biofilms on the implant surface that evade both antibiotics and host immune defences, so prosthetic joint infection often needs surgery.
